messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luis first remembers the accident like a cold splash of diesel and the sudden, sharp hiss of a collapsed pipe. He was thirty‑two inches below a high‑pressure copper line, tightening a valve on a rented two‑story apartment in East Los Angeles. The homeowner, a thirty‑five‑year‑old man, had been on the third floor when Luis’s wrench slipped, the metal chain he was holding falling onto the stairs and sending the man tumbling. Luis felt the impact of the body hit the landing, the house shudder, and the sound of a cracked arm. He froze, the world narrowed to the hum of the compressor and the thud of the falling man, and the image of the broken limb burned into his mind. From that moment he began to question whether his own body could ever be trusted to keep a hand on a tool or a foot on a ladder. He was certain that the accident was not only his fault but that his body had betrayed him. The shame of that realization has made him feel like a stranger in his own body. Because Luis has come to believe his body is unreliable and that he failed to prevent a tragedy, he has taken to avoiding anything that might remind him of that day. He skips birthday parties and the anniversary of July 14, the day of the accident, because the calendar itself feels like a threat. He also avoids the brief, stressful moments that come with deadlines on his job—tight deadlines for HVAC installations or unexpected breakdowns of a commercial system—because the very idea of a stressful situation feels like a precursor to another mishap. His mind goes over the accident in endless loops; he replays the exact angle of the wrench, the chain’s fall, the homeowner’s scream. He says the memory feels alien, as if a stranger’s body is reliving the pain. In the quiet of his apartment after a long day of work, he hears the hiss of the compressor and suddenly smells the faint, chemical scent of refrigerant that, in that instant, pulls the memory back into his consciousness. The memory surfaces unbidden, forcing its way into his thoughts whenever he hears silence or the whir of a fan. The moment the memory resurfaces, Luis feels the familiar tightness in his chest, his pulse racing, his sweat beginning to bead on his forearm. He feels as though the danger that killed the homeowner is still present, looming in the room like a silent threat. The sense of threat magnifies the memory’s intensity: the way the air smells, the echo of the homeowner’s pain, all heighten the feeling that something ominous is about to happen. The memory’s alien quality does not dull its impact; it simply reinforces the feeling that the past has taken hold of him, that he is haunted by a present danger. The silence that follows his breathing is a stark reminder of that same looming threat, a reminder that he must remain on guard. His avoidance has begun to cement his guilt. When he refuses to attend a company meeting or to accept a challenging job, he feels an even stronger sense of inaction guilt, convinced that each refusal is another failure to stop what could have happened. This guilt, in turn, keeps the sense of threat alive; he can no longer find a safe space because his avoidance has limited the places where he feels secure. The only spots he deems safe are his bedroom and the back porch where his mother lives, places where the world seems to pause and the silence feels less like an ominous signal and more like peace. Yet even in those few safe places, the memory can surface at any moment, a reminder that threat can be triggered by the slightest environmental cue. At work, the very environment that should offer structure instead triggers his physical reactivity. The quiet of a new apartment, the lack of ambient noise, can feel like a potential threat. Luis can be found on a ladder, clutching a wrench, his breathing shallow as the compressor starts up. He finds himself avoiding the noise of the compressor in new installations, the hiss that once reminded him of the accident’s diesel smell. In a week of refusing to take on a high‑profile project, his client became frustrated, and the client’s words were a sharp reminder of the threat he has been avoiding. The professional relationship strains, and Luis feels a growing fear that his avoidance of stress will leave him vulnerable at work and in his life. The day he finally sat in the therapist’s office was when he had to explain the new client’s refusal to come back for a scheduled service. He realized that the relationship strain had begun to affect his paycheck, and with it the stability of his living situation. What made him seek help was the realization that his avoidance had turned into a cycle of guilt, threat, and memory that no longer allowed him to function. He is most afraid that the pattern will never break and that he will continue to live in a state of hyper‑alertness, constantly feeling unsafe. Yet he also hopes that by confronting the tangled memories and the guilt he has carried, he might once again feel control in his own body and space.
